newsitem.title: GERMANY: INSTANT VIEW - German 1996, 1997 tax estimates.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - German 1996, 1997 tax estimates.

text.p: Following is a selection of economist comments on the German government's latest tax estimate, which forecast public sector revenues of 822 billion marks in 1997, down 10.3 billion marks from the previous tax estimate in May:

Noting that the economy had performed much better than the government predicted at the time of its May tax estimate, Schneider said the expected tax short-fall could be related to technical tax procedures, rather than weak growth.
"I would presume that there were some miscalculations (in the previous estimate). This is certainly not coming from the economy," he said.
Schneider added that he expected German gross domestic product to expand 1.5 percent this year and 2.5 percent next year.
The new estimates of lower tax revenue were "in line with expectations ... There have been so many changes in the tax laws."

The new estimate reflects 8.8 billion marks in revenue lost to the states from the striking of the wealth tax, Nerb noted. This will be largely offset by tightening the inheritance tax and other taxes.
Recent upward revisions in economic growth projections for 1996 and 1997 are not reflected in the tax estimate, but Nerb said this too is normal.
"It is not surprising because tax revenues are always lagging indicators. When the economy picks up this is not always immediately translated into higher tax revenues."
The 1997 federal deficit will perhaps be a bit higher than Finance Minister Theo Waigel's 56.5 billion mark target, but it will come close, despite the revenue shortfalls, Nerb said.
Federal revenues are still projected to rise to 344.9 billion marks in 1997 from 340.5 billion marks this year.
